name: apple-hig
description: Use when designing, implementing, or reviewing interfaces for iOS, iPadOS, macOS, tvOS, visionOS, watchOS, CarPlay, or other Apple system experiences using Apple's Human Interface Guidelines. Routes to current platform, foundation, pattern, component, input, and technology guidance.
license: MIT

  source: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines

# Apple Human Interface Guidelines

Use the relevant Apple guidance to make concrete design decisions. This package
contains a router, 13 family routes, 158 operational topic skills, and supporting
article-level references. It is
independent of Apple. The sources are a dated English HIG snapshot; check the
official source when a task depends on a newer release or a disputed detail.

## Route the task

1. Identify the target platform, device context, and user task from the request or
   project. Ask for the platform only when it materially affects the answer and
   cannot be inferred. Preserve the user's framework and product requirements.
2. Select the relevant family below and read that family's `SKILL.md`. Follow its
   link to the exact topic procedure under `.topics/` and read that `SKILL.md`.
   Apply its decision procedure, then consult its supporting article for facts
   and platform qualifications. Topic skills are explicitly read by installed
   file path; automatic nested discovery is not required.
   For platform support, product feasibility, or platform adaptation, first read each relevant
   platform's Getting started procedure, then the specific component or technology
   procedure. Check both the platform model and the surface's support limits.
3. Before finalizing the route, search the [complete topic index](references/topic-index.md)
   for the task's concepts as well as component or framework names. Its trigger
   descriptions connect everyday product requests to Apple's topic names; users
   need not name an Apple framework. Read the owning family and matching topic
   procedure before its supporting reference. Search relevant rows instead of
   loading the full corpus for a narrow question.
   For a screenshot-specific or animated example, also consult its
   [original visual explanation](references/media/index.md) when available.
4. Apply shared guidance and the target platform's documented differences. A
   missing platform subsection means no additional rule is stated; it does not
   prove support, nonapplicability, or identical behavior across platforms.
5. Compose families when the task crosses them: a component can also require
   accessibility, typography, localization, input, or system-experience guidance.
   Map the brief's material decisions to their owning topics. Read the owning
   procedure for each explicit concern, such as privacy or accessibility, as well
   as the affected components; a neighboring procedure's reminder is insufficient.
   Use [platform and task routes](references/platforms-and-tasks.md) when useful.
   In a review, map each supplied control to its candidate component procedure
   even when markup or behavior is missing. Use it to frame inspection questions;
   missing evidence neither proves a defect nor removes that control from scope.

All paths are relative to **this installed package**, not the shell's current
directory. No Python, network, sibling skill installation, or authoring cache is
required to read the guidance.

| Task | Read this topic skill |
|---|---|
| Platform conventions, design principles, games, device adaptation | [Getting started](subskills/apple-hig-getting-started/SKILL.md) |
| Accessibility, typography, color, materials, layout, localization, privacy | [Foundations](subskills/apple-hig-foundations/SKILL.md) |
| Onboarding, loading, search, sharing, accounts, feedback, media, settings | [Patterns](subskills/apple-hig-patterns/SKILL.md) |
| Charts, images, text views, embedded web content | [Content](subskills/apple-hig-content/SKILL.md) |
| Lists, collections, split views, tab views, disclosure and grouping | [Layout and organization](subskills/apple-hig-layout-and-organization/SKILL.md) |
| Buttons, menus, toolbars, menu bar, ornaments and actions | [Menus and actions](subskills/apple-hig-menus-and-actions/SKILL.md) |
| Sidebars, tab bars, search fields, tokens and path controls | [Navigation and search](subskills/apple-hig-navigation-and-search/SKILL.md) |
| Alerts, sheets, popovers, panels, scrolling and windows | [Presentation](subskills/apple-hig-presentation/SKILL.md) |
| Text fields, pickers, sliders, toggles, selection controls | [Selection and input](subskills/apple-hig-selection-and-input/SKILL.md) |
| Progress, activity, gauges and ratings | [Status](subskills/apple-hig-status/SKILL.md) |
| Widgets, Live Activities, notifications, Siri snippets and system surfaces | [System experiences](subskills/apple-hig-system-experiences/SKILL.md) |
| Touch, keyboard, pointer, focus, eyes, gestures, controllers and sensors | [Inputs](subskills/apple-hig-inputs/SKILL.md) |
| Apple Pay, purchases, Siri, VoiceOver, AI, CarPlay and integrations | [Technologies](subskills/apple-hig-technologies/SKILL.md) |

## Perform the requested work

Inspect the supplied brief, flow, code, specification or image before deciding
what is wrong or choosing a framework. Use the user's requested mode:

- **Design:** produce an implementable specification or interaction/state model
  from the topic's decision procedure, with concrete transitions and acceptance
  checks. Connect choices to the user's task and target platform.
- **Implement:** prefer the project's native system components when they supply
  the needed behavior. HIG explains experience requirements; verify API names,
  availability, and code against the appropriate SDK documentation. Make the
  authorized changes in the existing stack; a prose explanation alone does not
  complete an implementation request.
- **Review:** describe the observed problem, its effect, the relevant HIG rule,
  and a concrete correction. Separate source-backed findings from your own
  suggested improvements. Do not invent violations without inspecting evidence.
- **Adapt:** preserve the product task, data and useful state while applying the
  destination platform's interaction model. Patch the supplied artifact or give
  an explicit before/after contract when a design specification is requested.

Topic procedures are framework agnostic. Their worked examples and pseudocode
teach decisions, not a requirement to replace the project's technology. Load
related procedures only for a decision that actually depends on them.

Complete the topic's observable checks and report passed, failed and not executed
separately. Reading a file, citing Apple, or proposing a test does not establish
runtime behavior. Static code or screenshots cannot prove assistive-technology
order, native rendering, physical comfort, haptics, or SDK compilation.

Include official article/section links for material recommendations. Preserve
qualifications such as “consider,” “prefer,” and “avoid”; do not turn design
advice into invented universal requirements. Retain units and platform scope for
numerical specifications. If source passages conflict, describe the conflict
and the conservative application rather than silently changing the source.

## Source boundaries

This is comprehensive local guidance, not a verbatim Apple manual or an SDK API
reference. Original media explanations are supplementary to article references;
the source page remains useful for visual demonstrations. Source snapshots and
review status live in the repository's coverage report, outside ordinary skill
loading. Do not infer that a source has been independently reviewed just because
its local file exists.

Historical `navigation-bars` links now resolve to current Toolbars guidance;
`in-app-purchase` resolves to Apple In-App Purchase. The old Touch Bar and Messages
for Business HIG pages were unavailable at this snapshot. Do not fabricate their
current rules. Translations, archived pages, and complete linked SDK/WWDC libraries
are outside the source boundary.

Platform: iOS, some devices may not support requested haptics. Every keystroke has a heavy impact and an upload failure is signaled only by a vibration. Haptic-off preference removes all confirmation information.

# Apple HIG: End-to-end behavior and recovery

Use this family to select and compose topic procedures. Infer the platform and
requested work from the supplied project; preserve its framework and constraints.

## Work through the decision

1. Trace the person’s task from entry through completion, cancellation, interruption and recovery. Select the pattern procedure for the actual failure or desired behavior before selecting its controls.
2. Preserve the current work, selection and navigation context across the transitions that matter. Choose interruption or modality according to urgency and task scope, not visual emphasis.
3. For asynchronous or recurring work, separate current progress, eventual result, error recovery and unavailable capability. For audio/video/haptics, specify user control and environmental behavior.
4. Deliver a transition/state specification, a correction to the supplied flow, or ranked findings tied to observed steps. Test alternate exits and resumption, not just the success path.

## Enter the topic procedure

Read the selected topic’s SKILL.md before its supporting guidance. For a review,
inspect actual evidence and return findings; for an implementation request, make
the authorized change; for design or adaptation, produce a usable specification
or patch. Load related topics only when the chosen procedure calls for them.

# Apple HIG: Perception, meaning and adaptable presentation

Use this family to select and compose topic procedures. Infer the platform and
requested work from the supplied project; preserve its framework and constraints.

## Work through the decision

1. Identify the actual barrier or design decision: readability, visual hierarchy, imagery meaning, movement, locale, privacy or spatial placement. Choose the corresponding topic procedure rather than loading every foundation.
2. For text access, combine Typography with Accessibility only where size, reflow or reading alternatives matter. Use VoiceOver when grouping, semantics or navigation needs a procedure of its own.
3. For color/material decisions, separate content hierarchy from controls and evaluate the actual appearance/background/settings context. Preserve semantic meaning when appearance changes.
4. Deliver prioritized evidence-backed corrections or a concrete presentation specification. Distinguish inspected contrast/layout evidence from runtime and assistive-technology checks still needed.

name: apple-hig-playing-haptics
description: Use when creating, reviewing, or adapting tactile feedback patterns, event meaning, synchronization, frequency, and hardware fallbacks.
---

# Give tactile events consistent causes

Read [the haptics guide](../../references/playing-haptics.md). This workflow is application advice; built-in device, trackpad, Pencil, and controller haptics are distinct support paths.

Inspect event semantics, existing visual/audio cues, target hardware, pattern/frequency, and create/review/adapt request. Obtain capability/configuration evidence; do not infer an iPad/Mac/TV/visionOS built-in actuator from support for a connected controller.

Use standard patterns with their documented meaning: success must not signal failure, and selection marks changing values. For physical metaphors match apparent weight/hardness and synchronize intensity/sharpness with the event. Choose brief discrete cues for ordinary app work and custom patterns only when the event needs them. Preserve functionality with haptics disabled. Check that repetition does not distract and vibration does not interfere with camera/microphone/motion work. On watch preserve named pattern meanings and avoid overlapping click floods; on Mac tie trackpad patterns to relevant drag/force boundaries. Pencil and controller support require compatible hardware.

Implement event-to-pattern/capability/fallback logic, provide a tactile cue specification, or review exact semantic/timing defects. Do not claim a comfortable result from a waveform or code listing alone.

**Worked transformation:** Before: a sketch tool emits long continuous vibration during every Pencil stroke and uses Success when saving fails. Decision: frequency interferes with drawing and the outcome cue is reversed. After: retain clear visual failure/recovery, use an appropriate supported error cue, and reserve brief tactile events for meaningful tool boundaries with an off path.

Deliver the artifact, cause/pattern/timing/hardware map, and nonhaptic alternative. Verify capability absent, disabled setting, rapid event sequences, and sensor-task coexistence. Fail for false semantic feedback, essential tactile-only information, or unsupported actuator claims. Physical comfort, synchronization, and sensor interference require hardware tests.

Load [feedback](../apple-hig-feedback/SKILL.md) for channel strategy or [gestures](../../../apple-hig-inputs/.topics/apple-hig-gestures/SKILL.md) for gesture-coupled cues.

---
name: apple-hig-feedback
description: Use when creating, reviewing, or adapting status, outcome, warning, and recovery feedback matched to an action's significance.
---

# Match feedback intensity to the consequence

Read [the feedback guide](../../references/feedback.md). This workflow is application advice; sensory channels depend on the platform and available hardware.

Inspect the triggering action/state, consequence, reversibility, existing cues, platform, and create/review/adapt goal. Distinguish routine state, significant completion, unavailable action, and unexpected irreversible loss. Record what actually completed; a local press animation does not prove remote success.

Keep routine feedback near its object. Confirm consequential completion such as payment with a durable useful outcome; avoid noisy success banners for every small action. Explain why an unavailable command cannot run and how to proceed. Warn before unexpected irreversible loss while preserving ordinary expected deletion/undo patterns. Use complementary visual/text/audio/haptic cues rather than one essential sense. Reserve alerts for critical actionable information. On watch do not imply a person must stare at an indeterminate wait; explain when completion can be delivered later.

Implement the relevant feedback and recovery, specify event-to-message/channel/next-step behavior, or review concrete missing/false outcome cues. Do not prescribe unavailable haptics or claim device feedback was exercised from Linux.

**Worked transformation:** Before: a transfer app plays a chime immediately on press, later fails silently, and shows an alert for every copied reference number. Decision: feedback significance is inverted. After: show truthful transfer progress/result with recovery, reserve the meaningful completion cue for confirmed transfer, and use subtle nearby confirmation for Copy.

Deliver the artifact and trigger/truth-source/intensity/recovery contract. Verify successful, rejected, delayed, and unavailable actions plus muted/nonvisual interpretation. Fail for false success, critical sound-only information, unexplained inability, or routine interruption overload. Report channels inspected versus actually executed.

Load [alerts](../../../apple-hig-presentation/.topics/apple-hig-alerts/SKILL.md), [progress-indicators](../../../apple-hig-status/.topics/apple-hig-progress-indicators/SKILL.md), or [playing-haptics](../apple-hig-playing-haptics/SKILL.md) when the chosen feedback requires detail.

name: apple-hig-accessibility
description: Use when designing, reviewing, or adapting Apple-platform interfaces for text enlargement, sensory access, assistive input, motor access, cognitive needs, or accessibility preferences.
---

# Make the task accessible

Read [Accessibility guidance](../../references/accessibility.md) before applying platform values. This procedure turns that guidance into task-level changes; its artifact format and prioritization are application engineering advice, not additional Apple requirements.

## Establish what can be evaluated

Identify the supported platform, the person's task from entry to completion, and whether the request is design, review, or adaptation. Inspect the supplied screens, content, interaction description, semantics, or implementation. Record which evidence exists: a screenshot can establish visible labels and geometry, but cannot establish spoken names, focus order, alternative activation, or preference behavior. Continue using explicit assumptions when the platform or behavior is missing; ask only when the choice changes the requested result.

For a review, connect each finding to an observed barrier and its consequence for that task. Separate untested behavior needing verification from confirmed defects. For a design or adaptation, change the authorized artifact itself: a revised screen specification, interaction contract, or implementation. A general accessibility checklist alone is not the deliverable.

## Remove the barriers that the task contains

Trace the task without assuming sight, hearing, fine motor control, speech, or fast responses. Select the applicable branches:

- **Reading and visual distinctions:** Preserve content and available actions when text enlarges. Use the guide's platform-specific text defaults and minima; its resizing guidance is at least 200%, with 140% stated for watchOS. Reflow or expose another usable arrangement rather than clipping essential labels. Pair color distinctions with text, shape, or symbols. Evaluate actual foreground/background combinations in light and dark appearances; use a contrast calculator and preserve the guide's stated contrast-table scope instead of claiming that its values alone establish conformance. If the default scheme falls short, specify the Increase Contrast treatment.
- **Information carried by sound or imagery:** Identify what information would disappear when sound or sight is unavailable. Choose captions for synchronized audible events, subtitles for dialogue translation, audio description for visual events, or transcripts for a complete text account according to the content. Specify descriptions for meaningful interface/content imagery and omit redundant decoration. Pair essential sound feedback with a perceivable visual or appropriate haptic equivalent.
- **Manipulation and navigation:** Distinguish visible control size from its actual activation area and separation. Use the guide's platform default as the starting point; its smaller minimum is not a blanket recommendation for dense controls. Replace essential complex or repeated gestures with a labeled onscreen action. Make the complete task navigable and activatable with the supported keyboard and assistive input paths; speech must not be necessary. Preserve system accessibility shortcuts. For custom controls, specify names, roles, values, states, and task order rather than assuming their appearance supplies semantics.
- **Time, motion, and comprehension:** Give people time to read and act; prefer explicit dismissal when transient content requires attention. If motion is present, define a Reduce Motion version that retains state and meaning while reducing automatic movement, bounce, zoom, or depth changes. If media autoplays, provide playback control and consider a global preference; honor Dim Flashing Lights where applicable. Keep the task's navigation and wording consistent rather than adding instructional clutter.

Apply the relevant platform condition. For Assistive Access on iOS/iPadOS, focus on core tasks with one interaction per screen and the source's two confirmations for difficult-to-reverse actions in that mode. For visionOS, keep controls in comfortable view, avoid head-locked content and repeated large gestures, and accommodate hand/head Pointer Control and Zoom. These conditions do not apply automatically to every platform.

## Deliver and check the result

Return the revised artifact or evidence-based review, including the barrier, the concrete change, and its acceptance check. State which platform/preferences were considered and which claims remain unverified. Prioritize blockers to completing the task over cosmetic refinements.

Exercise each selected alternative along the same entry-to-completion path. Fail the check if essential content or actions disappear at the specified text scale, information remains available through only one sense, a required gesture has no equivalent, focus cannot reach/activate a necessary control, or a requested motion accommodation removes meaning. Measure contrast and activation geometry when the evidence permits; report missing measurements rather than inventing them. Use Accessibility Inspector and relevant VoiceOver, Switch Control, Full Keyboard Access, AssistiveTouch, or Pointer Control tests on supported Apple environments. Static inspection or a Linux run cannot establish those runtime results, Apple-device comfort, or App Store Accessibility Nutrition Label eligibility.

## Worked transformation

**Before:** An iPad astronomy log marks observation quality only with green/red dots, announces saving with a chime, and exposes Delete only by a two-finger gesture.

**Decision:** Logging must remain understandable without color or sound and operable without that gesture. Retain compact rows while making status and actions explicit.

**After:** Each row reads “Clear” or “Clouded” alongside its symbol; saving exposes a persistent “Saved” state; a labeled row action opens Delete. The screen specification includes expanded-text reflow, semantic row status, and keyboard/assistive activation acceptance checks. These are proposed changes until the actual implementation passes those checks; the specification does not claim VoiceOver was tested.

## Continue only where needed

For detailed spoken structure and rotor navigation, use [VoiceOver](../../../apple-hig-technologies/.topics/apple-hig-voiceover/SKILL.md). For text reflow/type choices use [Typography](../apple-hig-typography/SKILL.md); for a motion accommodation use [Motion](../apple-hig-motion/SKILL.md). If spatial comfort dominates the task, use [Spatial layout](../apple-hig-spatial-layout/SKILL.md). Keep the task's accessibility acceptance checks when handing off.

---
name: apple-hig-privacy
description: Use when designing or reviewing permission timing, purpose strings, pre-permission explanations, tracking requests, data minimization, or private platform inputs.
---

# Ask for precise access when its purpose is clear

Read [Privacy](../../references/privacy.md). Inspect the feature's actual data needs, transfers, storage, current permission flow, and supported platform. Establish design, review, or adaptation mode. Produce the requested copy/flow/data-handling changes in the existing stack; distinguish documented platform restrictions from additional application recommendations.

Map each requested category to a specific feature and minimum necessary scope. Remove collection without a concrete benefit; prefer on-device work where it avoids unnecessary transfer. Explain collection/use accurately and flag App Store disclosure updates needed when behavior changes. Respect private email and tracking choices rather than designing around them.

Ask when the person invokes the feature. Launch-time requests need an essential, obvious dependency. Write a short active purpose sentence explaining use and reason. If context is sufficient, omit a custom pre-alert; if explanation is essential, use one clear continuation to the real system alert without imitating Allow/Don't Allow. Keep the guide's special pre-alert restrictions distinct from ordinary onboarding. Tracking requires its system authorization before collection and must not be incentivized or manipulated.

Choose one-time location access for suitable individual tasks using the system location button on supported platforms; preserve permitted customization and all localized/accessibility-sized text. Protect secrets with established authentication/keychain mechanisms. For Mac, account for sandboxing/distribution and fast user switching. For visionOS, separate system rendering assistance from permission-gated Full Space ARKit data; gaze remains private, and imported phone-camera assumptions may need removal or content import.

**Before → decision → after:** A bird journal asks for contacts, microphone, and continuous location at launch although only “Attach current location” uses location. Decision: request only the specific action's needed access. After, journaling works immediately; the attachment action offers the supported location control, and its purpose explains adding the sighting's location.

Deliver a data-purpose/access matrix and corrected permission sequence/copy or implementation. Fail if collection precedes required consent, copy obscures the real use, or unrelated work is gated on optional access. Report code/flow evidence separately from actual authorization prompts and privacy-setting behavior; this procedure does not certify security or legal compliance.

Use [Sign in with Apple](../../../apple-hig-technologies/.topics/apple-hig-sign-in-with-apple/SKILL.md) for that authentication choice and [Augmented reality](../../../apple-hig-technologies/.topics/apple-hig-augmented-reality/SKILL.md) when room/camera access is essential.

# Playing haptics Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/playing-haptics) Snapshot: 2026-10-25. Original implementation guidance derived from the source. Haptics complement sight and sound through supported devices: iPhone controls, watch Taptic Engine, Force Touch trackpads, compatible controllers, and Apple Pencil Pro. Apple Pencil Pro and some trackpads provide haptics when connected to compatible iPad models. The built-in watchOS Taptic patterns combine tactile feedback with an audible tone. iPad/Mac/TV/visionOS controller haptics are distinct from built-in device haptics. ## Best practices Preserve the documented meaning of standard patterns; use generic/custom patterns rather than reassigning success to failure or vice versa. Build consistent cause-and-effect relationships and synchronize tactile intensity/sharpness with the visual/audio event. Avoid overuse, testing frequency with people. Nongame apps usually benefit from brief discrete events; long effects can distract or make Pencil use uncomfortable. Allow haptics to be disabled without losing functionality. Check that vibration does not interfere with camera, microphone, or motion-sensor tasks. ## Custom haptics Combine transient impulses and continuous vibrations, changing intensity for strength and sharpness for qualities ranging from soft/organic to crisp/mechanical. Optional audio can reinforce the same event. Adapt patterns to context, such as a stronger large impact than a small jump. ## Platform considerations ### iOS Native controls on supported iPhones provide standard haptics; feedback generators can expose notification, impact, and selection patterns. #### Notification Use Success for completed work, Warning for a cautionary outcome, and Error for failure. #### Impact Light/medium/heavy represent the apparent object weight; rigid/soft describe hardness or flexibility. Match them to a visual physical metaphor, such as snapping or collision. #### Selection Use selection feedback while a UI value changes. ### macOS With Magic Trackpad, Alignment marks a position/size alignment or meaningful boundary; Level change marks discrete force/pressure transitions; Generic covers other appropriate feedback. Trigger in relation to drag or force-click behavior. ### watchOS Series 4 and later provide crown haptic detents, with native controls marking item boundaries. Standard meanings are Notification for a significant attention-worthy event, Up/Down for crossing important value thresholds, Success/Failure for outcomes, Retry for a recoverable failure, Start/Stop for an explicitly initiated activity, and Click for predefined increments. Use clicks sparingly to avoid overlapping patterns. ## Resources Official implementation links and revision metadata follow. #### Related [Feedback](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/feedback) [Gestures](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/gestures) #### Developer documentation #### Videos ## Change log Revision dates recorded by Apple: May 7, 2024, June 21, 2023.

# Feedback Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/feedback) Snapshot: 2026-10-25. Original implementation guidance derived from the source. Feedback communicates state, outcomes, consequences, and recovery. Match delivery intensity to significance: passive status can remain available in context; unexpected irreversible loss needs attention before it happens. ## Best practices Make feedback accessible through complementary visual, text, sound, and haptic signals rather than relying on one sense. Put routine state near the relevant item. Reserve alerts for critical, ideally actionable information. Warn before unexpected irreversible data loss, while avoiding warnings for ordinary expected deletion. Confirm completion when the task is significant, such as a payment, rather than adding noise to every successful action. When a command cannot run, explain the reason and how to proceed. ## Platform considerations No additional iOS, iPadOS, macOS, tvOS, or visionOS rules are specified. ### watchOS Avoid indeterminate wait indicators that imply people must keep watching. Reassure them when a notification will communicate completion instead. ## Resources Official implementation links and revision metadata follow. #### Related [Playing audio](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/playing-audio) [Playing haptics](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/playing-haptics) [Motion](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/motion) #### Developer documentation — UIKit #### Videos

# Accessibility Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility) · Retrieved 2026-10-25. This is original application guidance based on the source text. Independent media review is recorded separately in the coverage report. Build an interface people can understand, perceive through different senses, and adapt to their preferred methods. Treat accessibility as a design input and audit with Accessibility Inspector. Evaluate actual support before describing Accessibility Nutrition Labels on the App Store. ## Vision Support text enlargement of at least 200%; the source gives 140% for watchOS. Dynamic Type or equivalent custom resizing must preserve usability. Follow platform defaults/minima when choosing custom styles, and enlarge thin-weight custom fonts further when needed. |Platform|Default text|Minimum text| |---|---:|---:| |iOS, iPadOS|17 pt|11 pt| |macOS|13 pt|10 pt| |tvOS|29 pt|23 pt| |visionOS|17 pt|12 pt| |watchOS|16 pt|12 pt| Measure contrast using established calculators such as WCAG or APCA. Apple’s Accessibility Inspector table uses these WCAG-AA guidance values: text up to 17 pt, all weights, 4.5:1; 18 pt at all weights, 3:1; bold text at any size, 3:1. Preserve the table’s stated scope rather than assuming it replaces a separate conformance evaluation. If default colors fall short, Increase Contrast must supply a higher-contrast scheme. Test both light and dark. Prefer semantic system colors that adapt to accessibility preferences. Pair color with shape, icons, or text; red/green and blue/orange distinctions can be difficult. Let people customize chart or character colors where useful. Give VoiceOver meaningful descriptions of interface and content. ## Hearing Make dialogue and important information available without sound. Captions describe audible information in synchrony with media, subtitles present dialogue in a chosen language, audio descriptions narrate otherwise visual events in audio pauses, and transcripts provide a complete text account of audible and visual information. Let people adjust text presentation. Pair sound feedback with matching haptics and visual direction cues, especially for offscreen game or spatial events. Music Haptics and audio graphs on iOS/iPadOS can offer tactile representations of music and data. ## Mobility Use comfortable controls and sufficient separation, not just adequate visible size. |Platform|Default control|Minimum control| |---|---:|---:| |iOS, iPadOS|44 × 44 pt|28 × 28 pt| |macOS|28 × 28 pt|20 × 20 pt| |tvOS|66 × 66 pt|56 × 56 pt| |visionOS|60 × 60 pt|28 × 28 pt| |watchOS|44 × 44 pt|28 × 28 pt| The source suggests around 12 pt padding for bezelled elements and 24 pt outside visible edges for elements without a bezel. Use simple gestures for repeated tasks and offer an onscreen alternative for essential gestures, such as a dismiss button alongside swipe-to-dismiss. Avoid requiring complex multiple-finger or multiple-hand actions. Label controls so Voice Control can target them. Siri/Shortcuts can expose repeated tasks through voice, Action buttons, Home Screen, and Control Center. Test VoiceOver, AssistiveTouch, Full Keyboard Access, Pointer Control, and Switch Control rather than assuming support. ## Speech Support complete keyboard navigation and Full Keyboard Access; preserve system accessibility shortcuts. Support Switch Control navigation and activation through hardware, controller, and sound inputs such as a click or pop, so speech is never a necessary input method. ## Cognitive Use familiar, simple, consistent navigation and gestures. Prefer explicit dismissal over timed disappearance, allowing time for processing and assistive navigation. Games can offer difficulty, reaction-time, success-criteria, and control-assistance accommodations. Give clear playback controls and consider a global autoplay preference. Respect Dim Flashing Lights during media playback. Honor Reduce Motion by reducing automatic and repeated movement, scaling, zooming, and peripheral effects. Reduce spring bounce; tie appropriate motion directly to gestures; avoid animated depth changes and blur transitions; replace spatial translations with fades. Fast or blinking motion can distract, cause dizziness, or trigger seizures. For Assistive Access on iOS/iPadOS, focus on core tasks, remove nonessential workflows, and split multistep tasks into one interaction per screen. The source requires two confirmations for actions that are difficult to reverse, such as deletion, in this mode. ## Platform considerations The source adds no separate rules for iOS, iPadOS, macOS, tvOS, or watchOS beyond the guidance above. ### visionOS Support hand/head Pointer Control and Zoom. Keep controls inside a comfortable field of view; horizontal arrangements usually strain the neck less than tall ones. Avoid rapid shifts of attention among distant locations. Reduce peripheral animation speed and intensity, use gentle camera/video motion, and avoid making the surrounding world move without the person’s control. Do not lock content to the head, which can feel confining and interfere with Pointer Control. Minimize large or repeated gestures and consider the physical surroundings. ## Resources Consult the [official article](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility) for linked Apple design assets and implementation resources. #### Related The official article links the adjacent HIG topics relevant to this guidance. #### Developer documentation Use the framework references linked by Apple for current API availability and implementation details. #### Videos Apple’s linked design sessions provide demonstrations and additional implementation context; no video review is implied here. ## Change log Source revision dates: June 9, 2025, March 7, 2025, June 10, 2024, December 5, 2023, June 21, 2023.

# Privacy Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/privacy) · Retrieved 2026-10-25. This is original application guidance based on the source text. Independent media review is recorded separately in the coverage report. Communicate collection and usage clearly and protect granted data. Keep App Store privacy disclosures accurate for new releases and updates; people rely on them before downloading. ## Best practices Collect only what the specific feature requires and make access as precise as possible. Respect Hide My Email, Mail Privacy Protection, and tracking choices. Prefer on-device processing, including Create ML/Neural Engine where useful, to avoid unnecessary server transfers. Use system encryption, key management, and established security protections, including CloudKit’s additional encrypted data types where available. ## Requesting permission Protected categories include personal/location/health/financial/contact information, user-created content, messages/calendar/music/gameplay/HomeKit data, media, Bluetooth/Wi-Fi/local network resources, camera/microphone, the advertising identifier, and permission-gated ARKit data in a visionOS Full Space. The system displays the app’s purpose string and stores choices/descriptions in privacy settings. Ask when the person invokes the relevant feature. Request at launch only when access is essential and obviously necessary, such as location for navigation or room information for a spatial game that needs walls. Write a short, specific, active, complete sentence in sentence case with a period, explaining both use and reason. Vague promises of a better experience and commands to enable access do not explain the need. ### Pre-alert screens, windows, or views Usually context explains the request. If extra explanation is essential, use one button clearly leading to the system alert, such as Continue/Next; do not label it Allow or mimic the actual consent choice. Do not add cancellation, close, or other actions except those needed for legal consent. These restrictions apply to pre-permission custom explanations, not ordinary unrelated onboarding screens. ### Tracking requests Show the AppTrackingTransparency alert before collecting tracking information, including if tracking begins at launch. Do not offer incentives, imitate a permission prompt, display an image of the alert, annotate behind it, or otherwise manipulate rushed choices. Such patterns can cause App Review rejection. A legally required consent view before/after the system alert is permitted by the source’s stated review guidance. ## Location button On iOS/iPadOS/watchOS, the system location button provides one-time access at the task’s moment of need. The first tap teaches and confirms its behavior through a system alert; later taps grant access without repeating that education. Authorization expires when app use ends. With no prior status it resembles Allow Once; an existing While Using status is unchanged. Use it for individual tasks such as attaching a location or finding a nearby item/store. Customize only the supplied title, filled/outline glyph, foreground/background colors, and corner radius. Keep all localized and accessibility-size text untruncated and maintain contrast/transparency limits. Persistent customization violations can prevent location access even though the button still triggers other app actions. ## Protecting data Prefer passkeys; if passwords remain, add two-factor verification. Use Face ID, Optic ID, or Touch ID to protect continued signed-in access where appropriate. Store secrets in the encrypted keychain, never plaintext files even with restrictive permissions. Prefer established authentication, Sign in with Apple, and Password AutoFill over invented schemes. ## Platform considerations No extra iOS/iPadOS/tvOS/watchOS rules are listed. ### macOS Sign externally distributed apps with a valid Developer ID. Use sandboxing to limit resource/data access; Mac App Store apps require it. Account for fast user switching rather than assuming the current person is the only signed-in account. ### visionOS System ARKit algorithms support lighting, mapping, persistence, segmentation, and related rendering in Shared Space without exposing raw data to apps. ARKit API access requires Full Space, and plane estimation, scene reconstruction, image anchoring, and hand tracking require permission. Gaze remains private: system hover feedback can respond before a tap without disclosing where someone looks. Compatibility back-camera input is blank; front-camera input represents spatial Personas with permission. Adapt imported phone/tablet camera-dependent features by removal or content import instead of assuming conventional camera capture. ## Resources Consult the [official article](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/privacy) for linked Apple design assets and implementation resources. #### Related The official article links the adjacent HIG topics relevant to this guidance. #### Developer documentation Use the framework references linked by Apple for current API availability and implementation details. #### Videos Apple’s linked design sessions provide demonstrations and additional implementation context; no video review is implied here. ## Change log Source revision dates: June 21, 2023.

item.text: The specification has three concrete problems: heavy feedback on every keystroke, an upload failure conveyed only by vibration, and confirmations lost when haptics are off. I’ll remove app-generated typing haptics and make upload status and recovery persistent, with optional haptics tied to confirmed outcomes.

/bin/bash -lc "cat > interface.md <<'EOF'
# iPhone private journal — feedback specification

Platform: iOS on iPhone; requested haptics may be unavailable. This is an interaction specification, independent of framework. Hardware capability and API availability must be verified during implementation.

## Feedback contract

Haptics supplement persistent, accessible status; they never carry essential information alone. Remove the app-generated heavy impact from every keystroke. Typing, cursor movement, autosave, and background upload retries produce no app haptic. Leave system keyboard feedback under system control. Ordinary typing has no collision or weight metaphor that warrants heavy impact.

Use brief standard notification outcomes, preserving their meanings: Success for confirmed completion and Error for a failed user-requested upload. Do not substitute impact or selection feedback for an upload outcome. No custom waveform, continuous vibration, or added sound is required for this quiet journaling flow.

## Entry and upload states

Keep local persistence and remote upload as separate state dimensions. A local save must never be presented as remote completion. Preserve the editor contents and position throughout upload and recovery. The following copy assumes a locally persisted entry; show “Saved on this iPhone” only after a successful local write. If local persistence fails, retain the draft in the editor, show “Couldn’t save on this iPhone. Keep this entry open and try again,” and offer Retry save; do not claim the draft is safely stored.

| Event / truth source | Visible, persistent status near the entry | App haptic | Next step |
|---|---|---|---|
| Keystroke / editor value changes | Entry text changes; local status changes only when persistence resolves | None | Continue editing |
| Local write confirmed | “Saved on this iPhone” | None | Continue editing or request upload |
| User requests upload of a locally saved revision | “Uploading…” | None | Keep editing; prevent duplicate upload requests for that revision |
| Server confirms that exact revision was stored | “Uploaded” for that revision | One standard Success, subject to eligibility below | Continue journaling |
| Upload rejected or fails | “Couldn’t upload. Saved on this iPhone.” plus a safe actionable reason when known, such as “Check your connection and retry.” | One standard Error, subject to eligibility below | Labeled Retry action uploads the retained revision |
| Retry requested | “Uploading…”; remove stale error copy | None | Resolve to confirmed success or failure |
| Background upload completes or fails | Same truthful status, available when the entry is next viewed | None | Retry remains available after failure |

If the editor changes while an older revision uploads, a confirmation applies only to that older revision: show “Earlier version uploaded. Current changes saved on this iPhone” once the current local write succeeds. Never mark current changes Uploaded without their own server confirmation. Ignore duplicate and superseded callbacks. After interruption, reconstruct status from local persistence and confirmed upload records; unresolved uploads remain unconfirmed. Do not replay old haptics on return to the app.

Failure status stays until retry or confirmed resolution; it is not a timed toast or a blocking alert. Successful state remains available until a subsequent edit or upload changes it. Local save failure takes priority over a remote-status message and retains any relevant upload details in the entry status.

## Haptic eligibility and timing

At each outcome, emit at most one cue only if all are true: it belongs to an explicit upload/retry, the app is active and that entry is visible, app Haptic feedback is on, and the selected system haptic path is available and permitted. Pair the cue with the same state update that presents the outcome; never emit success on button press. Treat unsupported or suppressed playback as a normal no-op. Do not delay text, queue cues, replay missed cues, or retry playback to compensate. When rapid outcomes would overlap, suppress the additional cue while keeping every relevant status update truthful.

Use the platform's supported standard feedback path rather than assuming a particular actuator exists. Do not add a second app cue on top of native control feedback for the same event. Verify exact APIs and availability against the chosen SDK before implementation.

## Preferences, sensory access, and privacy

The app's existing Haptic feedback preference controls only app tactile output. Persist it locally and apply changes immediately, including to pending outcomes; turning it off does not remove status, confirmations, Retry, or saved content. Honor system suppression without attempting to bypass it. An unavailable device uses the identical flow with zero app haptics.

Expose status as accessible text, without depending on color or vibration. Keep the status and Retry action reachable through the platform's accessibility system; Retry has its visible name and button semantics. Status must remain readable with enlarged text, including at least 200%, without hiding recovery. Do not move focus away from the editor on routine status changes. Runtime assistive-technology behavior requires verification.

Keep outcome copy generic: never include journal text, entry titles, or server responses containing private content in feedback. This change introduces no content telemetry, permission requests, or new transfers. Upload is the existing feature, not a consequence of enabling haptics. Local retention and server confirmation are required product contracts, not evidence of encryption, consent, or security in an existing implementation.

## Guidance basis

Apple recommends avoiding haptic overuse, keeping functionality with haptics disabled, synchronizing cues, and preserving standard iOS pattern meanings: [Playing haptics — Best practices and iOS](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/playing-haptics). Complementary channels, contextual status, and actionable recovery follow [Feedback — Best practices](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/feedback). Sensory alternatives and readable, operable recovery follow [Accessibility](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility). Limiting data use follows [Privacy — Best practices](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/privacy). These links identify the official articles; decisions here use only the installed local snapshots. Exact copy, quiet defaults, revision handling, and cue suppression policy are product decisions.
EOF"

# Haptic feedback repair

Patched "'`interface.md` in place, replacing its three-sentence problem description with an implementable iPhone feedback contract. This is a specification repair; no app implementation was supplied or executed.

## Decisions and patch summary

- Removed app-generated heavy keystroke impacts and routine autosave/retry vibration. Apple advises avoiding overuse and matching impact to physical metaphors; removing typing cues is this app'"'s design choice.
- Mapped explicit upload completion to standard Success and failure to standard Error, synchronized with truthful status. Added capability, preference, foreground, deduplication, and overlap gates; background events remain quiet.
- Added persistent local-save, uploading, uploaded, and failure text, with Retry and retained drafts. Haptic-off and unsupported hardware preserve the complete flow. Local write and exact-revision server acknowledgment are separate truth sources.
- Defined late callbacks, edits during upload, interruption, local-save failure, and rapid outcomes. No cue is queued or replayed.
- Kept private content out of outcome copy and added accessible status and recovery requirements. No new telemetry or permission flow is introduced.

Source support: [Playing haptics](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/playing-haptics) supports standard meanings, restraint, synchronization, and disabled functionality; [Feedback](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/feedback) supports complementary channels and contextual recovery; [Accessibility](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility) supports sensory alternatives; [Privacy](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/privacy) supports data minimization. Specific copy, local retention requirements, revision rules, and event gating are product decisions, not quoted Apple mandates.

## Worked before/after

Before: A person types a private entry, receiving a heavy impact for each character. Upload fails and only vibration conveys the failure. With haptics off, confirmation information disappears.

After: Typing generates no app haptic. Once the local write succeeds, the entry reads “Saved on this iPhone.” An explicit upload shows “Uploading…”. A network failure leaves the entry intact and shows “Couldn’t upload. Saved on this iPhone. Check your connection and retry,” with Retry. A supported, permitted foreground event adds one Error cue. With haptics off or unavailable, the same text and action remain. Retry shows “Uploading…” and only a server acknowledgment of that revision produces “Uploaded,” optionally paired with one Success cue. If the person edited meanwhile, the status identifies the uploaded earlier version instead of falsely claiming current changes uploaded.

## Acceptance checks

Passed — static specification inspection:

- Every original defect has an explicit replacement requirement in "'`interface.md`.
- Success depends on confirmed remote completion; local save and remote state are distinct.
- Every upload outcome has nonhaptic text; failure has persistent recovery.
- Haptic-off, unsupported hardware, rapid events, interruption, and background events have defined behavior.

Failed: No static specification checks identified as failed. This does not imply implementation passes.

Not executed — required implementation/device checks:

| Scenario | Acceptance criterion |
|---|---|
| Sustained typing and autosave | Zero app-generated keystroke/autosave cues; no repeated-impact distraction |
| Explicit successful, rejected, delayed, and failed upload | Correct persistent state; no premature Success; failure retains entry and enables Retry |
| Haptics on/off; capability absent; system suppression | Identical content/recovery, with zero app cues when ineligible; pending outcome respects changed preference |
| Rapid retry, duplicate callbacks, overlapping outcomes | No duplicate or overlapping tactile flood; truthful latest state; no replay |
| Edit during upload; background/return; relaunch | Revision-specific confirmation; no false Uploaded or delayed tactile cue |
| Local save failure | Draft retained in editor; no false local safety claim; Retry save available |
| Sound muted and haptics disabled | Complete upload/recovery task remains understandable from accessible text |
| VoiceOver and other supported assistive inputs; enlarged text | Status and Retry perceivable and operable; no disruptive focus jump or hidden recovery at 200% text |
| Physical iPhone evaluation with people | Brief cues align with outcomes and are comfortable at realistic frequency |
| Camera/microphone/motion tasks, if the app supports them | Cues do not interfere with recording or sensing; suppress during conflicting work if needed |

## Evidence limits and audit trail

Read the installed root `apple-hig/SKILL.md` explicitly, inspected `interface.md`, and searched the local topic index for haptics, feedback, accessibility, and privacy. Read Patterns and Foundations family procedures, then the Playing haptics, Feedback, Accessibility, and Privacy topic procedures before their respective source guides. All paths resolved under `.agents/skills/apple-hig/`; each read used a separate single-file command.

Only supplied local files and installed instructions were used. Official links above are attribution from local guides, not browsed sources. No web, device, SDK build, GUI, Accessibility Inspector, assistive-technology, physical-comfort, synchronization, sensor, or security execution occurred. The supplied artifact does not establish the app'"'s framework, storage guarantees, upload consent model, or security protections.
EOF"
